pages.text: "Bzzzzzz!" Nana Yaw pulled his blanket over his head. The mosquito returned. "Bzzzzzz!" The next morning, his sister, Abena, found him complaining. "I hate mosquitoes!" he said. "They cause every fever in Ghana." Abena shook her head. "Not every fever is malaria, and not every mosquito carries malaria parasites." "How do you know?" "Our science teacher told us. Come to school early. We are investigating mosquitoes today." Nana Yaw's eyes widened. "Investigating? Like detectives?" "Exactly!"

pages.text: Madam Lamptey displayed an enlarged photograph of a mosquito. "Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites," she explained. "In humans, the parasites are commonly transmitted through bites from infected female Anopheles mosquitoes." Nana Yaw frowned. "So the mosquito is not the parasite?" "Correct. The mosquito can carry and transmit it." "Then why doesn't every mosquito bite cause malaria?" "Because not every mosquito is infected, and different mosquito species have different roles." Abena wrote in her notebook: Good detectives must identify the real cause.

pages.text: During a supervised walk around the school compound, the class noticed an uncovered container holding rainwater. "Look!" cried Nana Yaw. "Something is moving!" Madam Lamptey observed the water from a safe distance. "Those may be mosquito larvae. Mosquitoes develop through several life stages, and many species use standing water for their early development." "Then we should remove places where mosquitoes breed!" Abena said. "Where appropriate and safe, yes. Adults should manage water storage, drainage and sanitation properly." The class reported the container to the school caretaker.

pages.text: A few days later, Nana Yaw developed a fever. "Malaria!" he announced immediately. His mother placed a reassuring hand on his shoulder. "A fever can have several causes. We need a health professional to assess you." At the clinic, a health worker examined him and arranged an appropriate test. "Why test?" Nana Yaw asked. "Because symptoms alone do not reliably tell us whether someone has malaria," the health worker explained. Nana Yaw realized that even a good detective should not guess when reliable testing is available.

pages.text: After Nana Yaw recovered, his family reviewed how to reduce mosquito bites. They checked their insecticide-treated bed nets for damage and made sure they were used correctly. They also discussed window screens and the safe management of standing water. "Does a bed net make us completely safe?" Nana Yaw asked. "No single measure removes every risk," his mother replied. "We use recommended prevention measures and seek medical care when someone becomes ill."

pages.text: Back at school, Abena presented her findings. "Malaria is not caused by dirty water itself," she explained. "It is caused by parasites. Mosquito breeding sites can increase the number of mosquitoes, but the parasite and its transmission are the key parts of the disease." Madam Lamptey nodded. "Excellent distinction." Nana Yaw raised his hand. "Then cleaning the compound is useful, but it cannot replace testing and treatment." "Precisely."

pages.text: The class prepared a science exhibition. They built a large paper model showing the mosquito life cycle. Another group made a poster about recognizing illness and seeking professional care. Abena created a diagram explaining how malaria transmission occurs. Parents gathered around the displays. "These children are teaching us important things," one visitor said. Nana Yaw grinned. "And we have learned not to blame every fever on mosquitoes!"

pages.text: That evening, Abena closed her notebook. Case: The Mosquito Mystery. Evidence: Malaria parasites can be transmitted by infected mosquitoes. Prevention: Reduce bites and breeding opportunities using recommended measures. Important rule: Seek professional testing and care for suspected malaria. Nana Yaw peered over her shoulder. "Will you become a doctor?" "Maybe," Abena said. "Or a scientist who discovers better ways to prevent disease." "Then I will be your assistant." She laughed. "Only if you stop diagnosing every fever yourself!"

activities.question: What causes malaria?
options: Plasmodium parasites transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes
Every flying insect that buzzes at night
Drinking clean water after playing football
activities.explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites, which can be transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

activities.question: What organism causes malaria?
activities.explanation: The Plasmodium parasite is the organism that causes malaria.

activities.question: Which mosquitoes can transmit human malaria?
options: Only male mosquitoes that feed on nectar
activities.explanation: In humans, malaria parasites are transmitted through bites from infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

activities.question: Does every fever mean a person has malaria?
options: No; a fever can have several causes and needs medical assessment.
Yes; every fever is always malaria.
Yes; there is never a need to visit a clinic.
activities.explanation: No. A fever can have several causes, so a health professional and appropriate testing are needed.

activities.question: Which two measures help reduce malaria risk?
options: Correct use of treated bed nets and reducing suitable breeding sites
Guessing illnesses at home without visiting a clinic
activities.explanation: Using insecticide-treated bed nets correctly and safely reducing mosquito breeding sites help lower malaria risk.

activities.question: Why is medical testing important when someone has a fever?
options: Symptoms can have different causes, so testing supports diagnosis.
Testing is only done for fun after someone recovers.
Symptoms alone always tell the exact cause.
activities.explanation: Because symptoms alone do not reliably identify malaria, testing supports accurate diagnosis and treatment.

glossary.definition: Organisms that live in or on another organism and can cause disease, such as Plasmodium.
Passed or carried from one person or organism to another.
The immature, wingless early stage of insects such as mosquitoes that hatch from eggs.
Systems and practices that keep water, drainage and surroundings clean and healthy.
Signs of illness felt by a person, such as fever, headache or tiredness.
Actions taken to stop a disease or problem from happening or spreading.
